section_summary: This section combines public appeals for restricting American exports to Japan with State Department replies explaining why the Neutrality Act had not been invoked and why non-munitions commodities could not legally be embargoed. It also contains diplomatic and military intelligence on Japanese purchases of trucks, aircraft, metals and other strategic supplies, including reports on Italian aircraft deliveries. A major Osaka consular report examines the rapid expansion of Japan’s armament industry and the conversion of small and medium-sized factories to war production.

subfiles.title: Reply to Fred H. Townsend on the Neutrality Act and exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Townsend’s additional views on applying the Neutrality Act and on shipments of scrap iron, cotton and oil to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green acknowledges Townsend’s May 16 letter and thanks him for supplementing his views. He promises that the arguments concerning the Neutrality Act and commodity shipments to Japan will receive careful consideration.

subfiles.title: Eugene Herring’s appeal to President Roosevelt concerning the Far East
subfiles.about: A heavily garbled handwritten appeal asks the President to address American involvement in the Far Eastern crisis.
subfiles.summary: The letter expresses concern about the conduct of the United States in relation to the conflict in the Far East. Although much of the handwriting is illegible in OCR, the accompanying reply identifies it as Herring’s May 16 communication about the regional situation.

subfiles.title: Reply to Eugene Herring explaining the Neutrality Act
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains why the President had not proclaimed a state of war between China and Japan under the Neutrality Act.
subfiles.summary: The Department states that a presidential proclamation would stop arms exports to both China and Japan, but that no legal authority existed to prohibit exports to Japan alone without one. It adds that the statute did not authorize restrictions on commodities other than arms and that the President had judged invocation contrary to the broader interests of the United States.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference on Canadian munitions shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Points to a report of the Canadian prime minister’s statement on aircraft and other exports to Japan and China.
subfiles.summary: The Canadian prime minister reportedly said that Canada’s only shipment to Japan during the crisis was one aircraft ordered beforehand, while only a few planes had been ordered for China. He also observed that total Canadian exports to Japan remained below their 1929 level.

subfiles.title: Transmission of Methodist resolution opposing aid to Japan
subfiles.about: Forwards a resolution adopted by the General Conference of the Methodist Episcopal Church, South.
subfiles.summary: Estes transmits the enclosed resolution under instructions from the denomination’s quadrennial General Conference at Birmingham. He closes with a pastoral blessing for the President.

subfiles.title: Methodist resolution against material and financial assistance to Japan
subfiles.from: General Conference of the Methodist Episcopal Church, South
subfiles.to: President and Congress of the United States
subfiles.about: Calls for measures preventing American public or private resources from aiding Japan’s war in China.
subfiles.summary: The resolution declares that Japanese forces have invaded China and that American war materials and supplies are contributing to Chinese suffering. It asks the President and Congress to prevent American material and financial resources from supporting Japan directly or indirectly.

subfiles.title: Reply to Lud H. Estes concerning the Methodist resolution
subfiles.from: Counselor, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges the General Conference resolution concerning shipments of war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department notes receipt through the White House of Estes’s letter and the April 30 resolution. It refers him to a May 16 State Department reply to his earlier letter on the same subject.

subfiles.title: Japan’s Military Imports
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Assesses the difficulty of estimating Japanese military imports omitted from official trade statistics.
subfiles.summary: Grew explains that military secrecy laws and the removal of numerous metals from published trade returns make non-recorded military imports nearly impossible to measure. Direct armed-service purchases such as fuel oil and munitions were also excluded, while consulates had found little useful information. The embassy had begun collecting fragments from technical sources and promised a later report on broad trends.

subfiles.title: Richmond boycott advocate’s letter on American supplies to Japan
subfiles.about: Urges Roosevelt to restrict American strategic exports that sustain Japanese aggression and military power.
subfiles.summary: Citing Eliot Janeway’s article “Japan’s Partner,” the writer argues that Japan depends on American oil, steel, nitrates and other commodities. The letter describes a Richmond consumer boycott and proposes coordinated action by the United States, Great Britain and Holland, while questioning the contradiction between arming Japan commercially and building a navy against it.

subfiles.title: Report on Japanese automobile imports and military truck orders
subfiles.from: Richard F. Boyce, American Consul, Yokohama
subfiles.about: Reports Japanese military commandeering and purchasing of Ford and other trucks for service in China and Manchuria.
subfiles.summary: Boyce reports that limited body-building capacity forced the military to commandeer civilian trucks and that further seizures had occurred in Hiroshima Prefecture. He estimates that thousands of trucks were operating in North and Central China with a comparable reserve in Manchuria, and notes a new order for roughly 2,000 Ford trucks. Trade figures also show direct United States shipments to Manchukuo outside Ford’s Japanese quota.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Foster Bain’s report on Philippine iron deposits
subfiles.about: Records Bain’s claim that Japanese interests sought to buy 50 million tons from newly identified Philippine iron deposits.
subfiles.summary: Foster Bain stated that substantial iron deposits had been found in the Philippines. He said Japanese interests wished to arrange the purchase of 50 million tons, a report informed by his recent mineralogical tour of China, the Philippines, Manchuria and Japan.

subfiles.title: Josh Lee’s forwarding letter to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Forwards constituent correspondence and asks the State Department to comply with its request if possible.
subfiles.summary: Lee submits an enclosed communication for Hull’s consideration. He asks that the letter be returned to his Senate office after the Department has disposed of the matter.

subfiles.title: W. C. Sawyer’s direct protest to Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Calls for immediate action by the United States and other democracies to stop war supplies reaching Japan.
subfiles.summary: Sawyer condemns Japanese bombing of cities and argues that diplomatic protests alone cannot stop attacks on civilians. He asks the United States to halt shipments still under its jurisdiction, seek parallel measures from other democracies and notify Japan of the action.

subfiles.title: W. C. Sawyer’s letter to Senator Josh Lee
subfiles.about: Asks Lee to investigate reports of discriminatory war-material shipments and to press for stronger action against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Sawyer reacts to a broadcast about the bombing of Hong Kong and reports that arms were allegedly flowing to Japan while shipments to China were held up. He asks Lee to present his demand for cutting off Japanese war supplies to the State Department.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull’s reply to Senator Josh Lee
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Lee’s referral of Sawyer’s letter and returns it with a copy of the Department’s response.
subfiles.summary: Hull acknowledges Lee’s June 9 communication enclosing Sawyer’s June 4 letter about exports to Japan and China. He supplies Lee with the response sent to Sawyer and returns the original constituent letter.

subfiles.title: Reply to W. C. Sawyer on arms exports to China and Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the Neutrality Act and compares licensed arms exports to China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department says that without a presidential state-of-war proclamation it cannot stop arms exports to Japan alone, while such a proclamation would embargo both belligerents. It reports licenses since July 1, 1937, of approximately $12.68 million for China and $9.29 million for Japan. The letter concludes that the President had determined that invoking the statute would not serve American interests.

subfiles.title: Harry F. Byrd’s forwarding letter concerning Warren Horton Stuart
subfiles.about: Forwards a former Virginian’s appeal concerning American assistance to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Byrd encloses a letter from Professor Warren Horton Stuart of the College of Emporia. He asks the Secretary of State to consider Stuart’s views.

subfiles.title: Warren Horton Stuart’s appeal against exports and loans to Japan
subfiles.about: Urges action against supplying Japan with oil, scrap iron, munitions or loans.
subfiles.summary: Stuart describes Japan’s campaign as an unjust attack on China and says American exports make the United States a partner in the destruction. He argues that cutting off essential supplies and credit would force the aggression to cease.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull’s reply to Senator Byrd
subfiles.about: Acknowledges Stuart’s letter and sends Byrd the Department’s reply and enclosures.
subfiles.summary: Hull identifies Stuart’s concerns about oil, scrap iron and munitions shipments to Japan. He encloses a copy of the response being sent to Stuart, together with its enclosures, and returns Stuart’s original letter.

subfiles.title: Reply to Warren Horton Stuart on exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the statutory limits on stopping exports to Japan and reiterates official condemnation of bombing civilians.
subfiles.summary: Green explains that invoking the Neutrality Act would halt arms exports to both China and Japan and that the law does not authorize an embargo on oil, scrap iron or other non-listed commodities. He gives comparative export-license totals and cites Hull’s June 11 condemnation of civilian bombing and its material encouragement. The letter assures Stuart that the government will continue using practicable means to discourage inhumane conduct.

subfiles.title: Sam Silver’s request for names of aircraft exporters to Japan
subfiles.about: Requests public identification of private corporations exporting warplanes and aircraft parts to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Silver welcomes Hull’s June 11 statement against supplying aircraft for indiscriminate bombing. He argues that public opinion could stop the trade and asks the Department to identify the corporations shipping planes and components to Japan.

subfiles.title: Reply to Sam Silver on confidential export-license details
subfiles.from: Charles W. Yost, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Declines to identify individual aircraft exporters while providing aggregate munitions-control publications.
subfiles.summary: Yost thanks Silver for supporting the government’s position on civilian bombing but refuses to disclose the names of individual exporters. He explains that the Department publishes monthly aggregate licensing statements while withholding individual license details, and encloses an annual report and the May 1938 press statement.

subfiles.title: Robert J. Bulkley’s forwarding letter concerning Miriam Rogers
subfiles.about: Forwards Miriam Rogers’s letter urging cessation of arms shipments to Japan and requests a comment for her.
subfiles.summary: Bulkley sends Hull a constituent letter from Miriam L. Rogers of Warren, Ohio. He asks for a State Department comment that he can transmit to her.

subfiles.title: Miriam Rogers’s appeal to stop war-material shipments to Japan
subfiles.about: Urges an end to American shipments of arms and all other war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Rogers appeals on grounds of humanity, Christianity and American self-interest. She warns that helping Japan defeat China would arm a future rival and threaten the Open Door and American trade in East Asia.

subfiles.title: Memorandum requesting approval of the draft reply to Bulkley
subfiles.about: Calls Hull’s attention to proposed written use of his June 11 remarks condemning civilian bombing.
subfiles.summary: The division notes that the Department had not yet issued a written account of Hull’s June 11 press-conference statements. Because the draft language might be reused in numerous replies, officials seek his specific approval before sending it.

subfiles.title: Draft reply to Senator Bulkley concerning Miriam Rogers
subfiles.about: Provides a suggested explanation of the Neutrality Act and Hull’s condemnation of civilian bombing for transmission to Rogers.
subfiles.summary: The draft says a presidential proclamation would embargo arms to both China and Japan, while no authority existed to single out Japan. It supplies comparative export-license totals and recounts Hull’s June 11 statement condemning attacks on civilians and the material encouragement of such attacks. Rogers’s original letter is returned.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Italian aircraft and ammunition supplied to Japan
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck and Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes military-attaché reporting on Italian bombers, artillery components and aviation personnel connected with Japan.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum reports a Japanese contract for 200 BR.20 bombers and 200 spare engines and evidence that at least 112 aircraft had been shipped. It also identifies a Borgomanero plant making artillery-projectile cases for Japan. Italian aviation personnel apparently went to Japan as civilian instructors or pilots rather than combatants, while most members of the former Italian mission in China had returned home.

subfiles.title: Military attaché report on Italian assistance to Japan
subfiles.doc_type: military intelligence report with routing sheet
subfiles.from: George N. Paine, Military Attaché, Rome
subfiles.about: Reports Italian aircraft shipments, ammunition production and aviation personnel associated with Japan and China.
subfiles.summary: Paine describes a contract for 200 Italian bombers and spare engines and records seeing four aircraft with serial numbers 109–112 crated at Marina di Pisa for Japan. He reports projectile cases being manufactured at Borgomanero for Japan and ammunition for Spain. He judges it unlikely that Italian Air Corps personnel were fighting with Japanese forces, although some may have served as civilian instructors or liaison personnel.

subfiles.title: Continued Expansion of Armament Industry
subfiles.from: John K. Emmerson, American Vice Consul, approved by George A. Makinson
subfiles.to: Supervising Consul General, Tokyo, and Department of State
subfiles.about: Analyzes the expansion of Japanese munitions production and the conversion of smaller industries to armament work.
subfiles.summary: The report compares orders and production capacity at major Japanese manufacturers, showing that demand for war materials greatly exceeded existing output despite rapid factory expansion. It describes government subsidies, technical supervision, industrial guilds and factory pooling intended to convert small and medium firms to munitions production while addressing shortages of capital, skilled labor and technical knowledge. Examples show civilian manufacturers abandoning ordinary products for military equipment, and the conclusion argues that effective armament production could determine the survival of Japan’s small-industry system.

subfiles.title: Telephone memorandum on planned Washington peace delegation
subfiles.about: Reports plans for a delegation demanding prohibition of war-supply shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Miss Loomis relays a telegram stating that peace societies, church groups and others planned to travel to Washington. The delegation intended to press the government to prohibit shipments of war supplies to Japan; Earl Leaf’s New York information exchange was coordinating supportive organizations.

subfiles.title: Edward H. Hume’s telegram supporting an embargo
subfiles.about: Supports State Department pressure on aviation manufacturers and calls for a complete embargo on war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hume expresses approval of pressure on aviation-material manufacturers. He says he has also telegraphed the President and Hull in support of China-relief organizations seeking a comprehensive embargo.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck’s acknowledgment to Edward H. Hume
subfiles.about: Acknowledges and appreciates Hume’s supportive telegram.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck thanks Hume for the message sent on June 13. The response is cordial but does not address the requested embargo in detail.

subfiles.title: Further report on Japanese military commandeering of trucks
subfiles.about: Supplies additional reports of used trucks commandeered by Japanese military authorities.
subfiles.summary: Boyce reports further seizures of trucks in several Japanese localities, including Yokohama, Chiba and Tokyo. The clearest figure states that roughly 1,000 used trucks had recently been commandeered in Tokyo. Copies were distributed to the embassy, State Department, consulate general and military attaché.

subfiles.title: Edward H. Hume’s letter urging pressure on exporters to Japan
subfiles.about: Advocates category-by-category pressure on manufacturers exporting vehicles, fuel and aviation materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hume cites continued bombing of American property and Japanese efforts to define a vast Chinese war zone east of a line from Xi’an to Hainan. He notes fears that Japan might formally declare war to force neutral countries to invoke their neutrality laws. He nevertheless argues that vigorous State Department pressure could persuade manufacturers to curtail strategically important exports.

subfiles.title: Reply to Edward H. Hume on war-material exports
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the Neutrality Act’s limits and directs Hume to Hull’s statement on sales of aeronautical equipment.
subfiles.summary: Green states that a presidential proclamation would prohibit arms exports to both China and Japan, while the law provided no power to embargo Japan alone or to stop non-munitions commodities. He says the President had concluded that invoking the resolution was not in the broader American interest. Updated license totals are supplied, and Hume is referred to Hull’s June 11 comments concerning aircraft sold to governments bombing civilians.

subfiles.title: Tom Connally’s forwarding note to the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent communication for favorable consideration and requests a report.
subfiles.summary: Connally transmits an enclosure to the State Department. He asks that the Department report its disposition and return the enclosed letter to his Senate office.

subfiles.title: Nellie M. Broderson’s appeal against sales to Japan
subfiles.about: Urges Connally to stop sales of bombing planes and other war materials to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Broderson condemns American sales that contribute to the destruction of defenseless Chinese civilians. She contrasts those exports with American charitable appeals for Chinese relief and calls the policy morally inconsistent and greedy.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull’s reply to Senator Connally
subfiles.about: Provides materials and an explanation of the Neutrality Act for transmission to Broderson.
subfiles.summary: Hull explains that a presidential proclamation would halt arms exports to both China and Japan and that no authority existed to impose a unilateral embargo on Japan. He gives license totals for both countries and recounts his June 11 condemnation of civilian bombing and its material encouragement. The enclosed pamphlet, congressional resolution and Broderson’s original letter are supplied to Connally.

subfiles.title: Nathan Alexander’s appeal to President Roosevelt
subfiles.about: Asks Roosevelt to stop American war-material sales to Japan after attacks on Chinese civilian centers.
subfiles.summary: Alexander cites news photographs and reports of Japanese bombing and asks how the United States can continue furnishing war materials. He asserts that decisive presidential action would be popular and supported by the country.

subfiles.title: Reply to Nathan Alexander on exports to Japan
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains why the Neutrality Act had not been invoked and why it could not prohibit ordinary commodities.
subfiles.summary: Green states that a proclamation of war would embargo arms to both China and Japan, while no authority existed to prohibit exports to Japan alone. He adds that the act did not cover commodities outside the statutory munitions list and that the President had judged invocation contrary to American interests. Comparative export-license totals are included with copies of the resolution and an explanatory pamphlet.

subfiles.title: Chevy Chase Presbyterian Church telegram to Cordell Hull
subfiles.from: Arthur T. Pienkowsky, for the Session of Chevy Chase Presbyterian Church
subfiles.about: Supports official condemnation of bombing civilians and opposes current war-supply shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The church session aligns itself with the government’s condemnation of bombing civilian populations. It also joins other organizations in condemning continued shipments of war supplies to Japan.

subfiles.title: White House referral of the Chevy Chase Presbyterian Church telegram
subfiles.about: Forwards the church’s duplicate telegram condemning civilian bombing and war-supply exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The referred copy repeats the Chevy Chase Presbyterian Church session’s support for condemning attacks on civilians. It also records the session’s opposition to shipments of war materials to Japan.

subfiles.title: Reply to Arthur T. Pienkowsky and the Chevy Chase Presbyterian Church
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acknowledges both copies of the church telegram and explains the government’s Neutrality Act position.
subfiles.summary: The Department thanks the church for supporting its condemnation of civilian bombing and acknowledges both the direct telegram and the White House referral. Green explains that invoking the Neutrality Act would embargo China as well as Japan, that ordinary commodities were outside the law and that the President had declined to invoke it in the national interest. The letter supplies comparative export-license figures and encloses the relevant congressional resolution and pamphlet.
